lines: The ford east of the village is gone. The creek took it before the thunder stopped.
I spent the morning checking which landmarks were struck and which only looked different in the rain.
Three paths flooded at once, so we marked the safest doorways instead.
Lightning burned the old oak into a better warning sign than I ever wanted.
My neat road lines mean little when the road itself is under water.
The storm washed the chalk marks off every doorstep on the east lane.
I used the highest windows to see which roads were flooding.
A fallen branch turned the north road into a dead end.
The bridge held, but the banks on both sides did not.
I have marked three roofs where lightning struck close enough to matter.
The compass needle twitched with every nearby strike.
I weighted the loose charts with stones before the wind took them.
Lightning showed the eastern road in flashes, then left it black again.
The rain moved two path markers before morning.
One flooded ditch made the south road useless for carts.
I marked the fallen branches while the route was still fresh in everyone's mind.
Wet parchment can be copied. A traveler caught outside cannot.
We used the map table to plan which homes needed checking first.
The storm changed the creek enough that my old line is wrong now.
When the thunder passed, I walked every road that still looked safe.
Smoke made the village feel like a place I had <dark_gray><wavy>never mapped</wavy></dark_gray>.
I pointed the bucket line through the garden because the lane was already burning.
The old charts nearly went up, but I left them when someone called from the next room.
We found two ways to the well and needed both of them.
Every burned doorway is marked now, along with the safest way around it.
The smoke erased every landmark above the roofs.
I marked a clear route for people carrying water back from the well.
We used the open field as a meeting place because every lane felt too narrow.
A burning fence closed the quickest way between two homes.
I will never draw those roofs so close together again.
Dry maps burn quickly, so we carried the oldest copies outside first.
Smoke hid the square well enough to make familiar doors hard to find.
I drew a quick route for the bucket line when people started colliding.
The wind pushed sparks toward the roofs along the west road.
We cleared the lane so nobody had to choose between a wall and the flames.
One map frame caught fire after everyone thought the room was safe.
Ash settled on the compass glass until north looked gray.
I marked every damaged building before the cleanup moved the evidence.
The shortest path to the well was blocked, so we used the garden gate.
The new village map will include wider fire breaks between those roofs.
The raiders came through the orchard where my map showed open ground.
I sent families through the narrow paths the raiders had not noticed.
The bell gave us just enough time to close the gate by the fields.
A clear road became dangerous the moment their crossbows reached the square.
Their retreat left a line of tracks I intend to remember.
I watched their line split where the market road bends.
The map room became the place everyone used to check which houses were clear.
A broken gate erased the retreat line I had planned.
The raiders ignored the steep path until villagers used it to escape.
I kept one finger on the road home while the horns were sounding.
The raiders used the shallow ditch I had dismissed as useless ground.
I marked their first sighting and every place the line split afterward.
From the mapping room window, the north lane became a straight shot to the square.
We moved families along the back paths before the raiders closed them.
One alley looked safe on paper and trapped three defenders behind a cart.
The bell gave us time to close the western route.
I kept track of which houses had already been searched.
Their banners were visible from farther away than their crossbows were.
The retreat path tells me where they may approach next time.
I have drawn three new warning marks beyond the village border.
Something put out the last torch by the fields before the bell rang.
I knew the lanes, but shouting made every turn feel wrong.
We guided people by knocking on walls when carrying lamps became too dangerous.
At dawn, the broken fences told the story better than anyone could.
I am marking every place where darkness reaches past the road lamps.
I marked the last place each missing villager had been seen.
The road lamps left wide gaps where attackers could move unseen.
A familiar fence became our best guide through the dark.
We found the safest route only after the main lane was blocked.
I am redrawing the shelter paths so none cross open ground.
Darkness erased the space between the last torch and the fields.
I knew the lanes by memory, but fear added turns that were not there.
We used chalk arrows so people could find the shelter without lamps.
The attackers came from the road with the fewest clear sightlines.
A rooftop watcher called directions while the rest of us stayed below.
I marked every broken fence before sunrise hid the fresh tracks.
The moon put the eastern wall in silhouette and left the gate invisible.
One dropped torch showed us a path nobody should have been using.
By dawn I could trace their movement from footprints and damaged doors.
Tonight the outer road gets twice as many lamps.
The first gust erased the cart tracks and the second buried the road markers.
We moved from doorway to doorway because there was no longer a square to cross.
North still meant north, but that did not help us see the well.
I kept a hand on the wall and counted corners until I found the mapping room.
The whole eastern approach has a new shape now.
I put the map away and followed the fence like everyone else.
The dunes crossed the road faster than anyone could mark them.
One buried sign left three families arguing over the same turn.
We scratched arrows into doorframes where the wind could not erase them.
The old well became our only useful landmark.
The compass stayed useful after every road vanished under sand.
I tied the map case shut because grit had already reached the table.
We followed walls instead of paths when the square disappeared.
The north marker was buried to its top before the wind eased.
A familiar walk to the well felt like crossing blank country.
I counted doorways aloud so nobody passed their own shelter.
Sand reshaped the low road enough that carts will need another route.
The wind uncovered an old stone line I had never mapped.
Every chart survived, though the hinges may never stop grinding.
I am redrawing the dunes before another traveler trusts yesterday's view.
The road signs disappeared while we were still bringing firewood inside.
We ran guide ropes between the busiest homes before the drifts grew deeper.
Knowing north did not tell us whether the snow ahead would hold.
Every trip to the well needed a fresh path and someone watching from the door.
I expect the spring map to look very different around the low road.
I marked warm houses instead of roads while the storm held.
A drift swallowed the east path and made the long lane safer.
We used chimney smoke to find homes beyond the square.
Every cleared door became a landmark for the next group.
I kept a small chart of who had enough firewood.
Snow buried the road signs before it buried the fences.
We tied a rope from the map room to the well and followed it by hand.
The compass gave direction, but it could not show which drifts would hold.
I marked each cleared doorway so nobody wasted strength digging twice.
White ground made the village look unfinished on every side.
A chimney was sometimes the only landmark left above the drifts.
The southern path moved uphill overnight because of packed snow.
We checked isolated homes in the order I could fit onto one small chart.
Fresh tracks mattered more than any old road until the wind covered them.
When the thaw comes, I expect half the lane markers to be somewhere new.
